claims.claim: NaV1.1 is referred to as a 'super culprit' gene, with over 1000 associated mutations that lead to abnormal brain function.
claims.source: Indeed, Scn1a, the gene that encodes NaV1.1, is referred to as a 'super culprit' gene, with over 1000 associated mutations that lead to abnormal brain function, resulting in brain disorders such as epilepsy and migraine, as well as neurodivergent phenotypes, such as autism spectrum disorder (Ding et al., 2021; Lossin, 2009).
claims.evidence: Cited from published literature (Ding et al., 2021; Lossin, 2009).

claims.claim: Homozygous Scn1a-/- global knockout mice are ataxic and die by postnatal day 15.
claims.source: Homozygous Scn1a-/- global knockout mice are ataxic and die by postnatal day (P) 15, while heterozygous Scn1a+/- animals develop seizures and begin to die sporadically starting at P21 (Yu et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: Cited from published literature (Yu et al., 2006).

claims.claim: Heterozygous Scn1a+/- global knockout mice develop seizures and begin to die sporadically starting at postnatal day 21.
claims.source: Homozygous Scn1a-/- global knockout mice are ataxic and die by postnatal day (P) 15, while heterozygous Scn1a+/- animals develop seizures and begin to die sporadically starting at P21 (Yu et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: Cited from published literature (Yu et al., 2006).

claims.claim: NaV1.1 is expressed in the peripheral nervous system.
claims.source: In addition to the central nervous system (CNS), NaV1.1 is also expressed in the peripheral nervous system (PNS) (Sharma et al., 2020; Usoskin et al., 2015); yet, the prominent role this channel plays in brain function has left its physiological roles in sensory neuron populations understudied.
claims.evidence: Cited from published literature (Sharma et al., 2020; Usoskin et al., 2015).

claims.claim: Scn1a transcript and protein have been observed primarily in myelinated mechanosensory DRG and TG neurons.
claims.source: Scn1a transcript and protein have been observed primarily in myelinated mechanosensory DRG and TG neurons (Fukuoka et al., 2008; Ho and O'Leary, 2011; Osteen et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: Cited from published literature (Fukuoka et al., 2008; Ho and O'Leary, 2011; Osteen et al., 2016).

claims.claim: Subcutaneous injection of the NaV1.1 activator, Hm1a, into mouse hind paw causes noninflammatory mechanical pain and spontaneous pain behaviors.
claims.source: Indeed, subcutaneous injection of the NaV1.1 activator, Hm1a, into mouse hind paw causes noninflammatory mechanical pain and spontaneous pain behaviors (Osteen et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: Cited from published literature (Osteen et al., 2016).

claims.claim: Pharmacological inhibition of NaV1.1 does not affect mechanical thresholds in uninjured mice but does reduce mechanical pain in a spared-nerve injury model.
claims.source: Interestingly, pharmacological inhibition of NaV1.1 does not affect mechanical thresholds in uninjured mice but does reduce mechanical pain in a spared-nerve injury model (Salvatierra et al., 2018), suggesting that NaV1.1 may have a more prominent role in mechanical pain as opposed to normal touch sensing.
claims.evidence: Cited from published literature (Salvatierra et al., 2018).

claims.claim: NaV1.1 in TG neurons mediates mechanical pain in an orbitofacial chronic constriction injury model.
claims.source: NaV1.1 in TG neurons has also been reported to mediate mechanical pain in an orbitofacial chronic constriction injury model (Pineda-Farias et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: Cited from published literature (Pineda-Farias et al., 2021).

claims.claim: NaV1.1 is found in colon-innervating vagal neurons, where it contributes to firing of colonic mechano-nociceptors and is upregulated in a mouse model of chronic visceral hypersensitivity.
claims.source: In addition to somatosensory neurons, NaV1.1 is found in colon-innervating vagal neurons, where it contributes to firing of colonic mechano-nociceptors and is upregulated in a mouse model of chronic visceral hypersensitivity (Osteen et al., 2016; Salvatierra et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: Cited from published literature (Osteen et al., 2016; Salvatierra et al., 2018).

claims.claim: NaV1.1 contributes to action potential firing in a subset of DRG neurons that express TRPM8.
claims.source: Lastly, NaV1.1 contributes to action potential firing in a subset of DRG neurons that express the cold-sensitive ion channel, transient receptor potential melastatin 8 (TRPM8), suggesting that the channel may also contribute to thermosensory transmission (Griffith et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: Cited from published literature (Griffith et al., 2019).

claims.claim: RNA-sequencing datasets have consistently identified NaV1.1 expression in proprioceptors.
claims.source: RNA-sequencing datasets have consistently identified NaV1.1 expression in proprioceptors; thus, we next analyzed NaV1.1 expression in these cells using a ParvalbuminCre;Rosa26Ai14 reporter line (PvalbAi14) and found that 100% of genetically identified proprioceptors were positive for Scn1a message (Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: Referenced as established knowledge from RNA-sequencing datasets.

claims.claim: NaV1.6 and NaV1.7 expression has been reported in proprioceptors.
claims.source: In addition to NaV1.1, NaV1.6 and NaV1.7 expression has also been reported in proprioceptors (Carrasco et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: Cited from published literature (Carrasco et al., 2017).

claims.claim: NaV1.1 is haploinsufficient in several brain neuron cell types for normal excitability and function.
claims.source: NaV1.1 is haploinsufficient in several brain neuron cell types for normal excitability and function (Ogiwara et al., 2007; Yu et al., 2006), suggesting the contributions of NaV1.1 to neuronal function are highly sensitive to genetic perturbations.
claims.evidence: Cited from published literature (Ogiwara et al., 2007; Yu et al., 2006).

claims.claim: Loss of a single copy of NaV1.1 is sufficient to attenuate sustained action potential firing in parvalbumin-positive hippocampal interneurons.
claims.source: Indeed, loss of a single copy of NaV1.1 is sufficient to attenuate sustained action potential firing in parvalbumin-positive hippocampal interneurons (Ogiwara et al., 2007; Yu et al., 2006) and cerebellar Purkinje neurons (Yu et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: Cited from published literature (Ogiwara et al., 2007; Yu et al., 2006).

claims.claim: Loss of a single copy of NaV1.1 is sufficient to attenuate sustained action potential firing in cerebellar Purkinje neurons.
claims.source: Indeed, loss of a single copy of NaV1.1 is sufficient to attenuate sustained action potential firing in parvalbumin-positive hippocampal interneurons (Ogiwara et al., 2007; Yu et al., 2006) and cerebellar Purkinje neurons (Yu et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: Cited from published literature (Yu et al., 2006).

claims.claim: NaV1.1 has been associated with persistent sodium current (INaP) and resurgent sodium current (INaR), both of which promote repetitive firing in a wide variety of cell types in the CNS and PNS.
claims.source: NaV1.1 has been associated with persistent sodium current (INaP) and resurgent sodium current (INaR), both of which promote repetitive firing in a wide variety of cell types in the CNS and PNS (Barbosa et al., 2015; Kalume et al., 2007; Khaliq et al., 2003).
claims.evidence: Cited from published literature (Barbosa et al., 2015; Kalume et al., 2007; Khaliq et al., 2003).

claims.claim: NaV1.1 recovers rapidly from fast inactivation compared to other channel subtypes.
claims.source: NaV1.1 also recovers rapidly from fast inactivation compared to other channel subtypes (Herzog et al., 2003; Patel et al., 2015) and has been shown to be refractory to entry into slow inactivation in TRPM8-expressing DRG neurons (Griffith et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: Cited from published literature (Herzog et al., 2003; Patel et al., 2015).

claims.claim: NaV1.1 has been shown to be refractory to entry into slow inactivation in TRPM8-expressing DRG neurons.
claims.source: NaV1.1 also recovers rapidly from fast inactivation compared to other channel subtypes (Herzog et al., 2003; Patel et al., 2015) and has been shown to be refractory to entry into slow inactivation in TRPM8-expressing DRG neurons (Griffith et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: Cited from published literature (Griffith et al., 2019).

claims.claim: Loss of synaptic-like vesicle released glutamate from afferent endings produces a similar deficit in static but not dynamic sensitivity.
claims.source: A similar deficit in static but not dynamic sensitivity was seen following loss of synaptic-like vesicle released glutamate from afferent endings (Than et al., 2021); however, in those afferents, firing only occurred at the beginning of stretch and patchy firing was never observed.
claims.evidence: Cited from published literature (Than et al., 2021).

claims.claim: Many epilepsy patients with hemizygous NaV1.1 loss of function display ataxia and motor delays and deficiencies.
claims.source: Notably, Scn1a is a super culprit gene with over 1000 associated disease-causing mutations, most of which are linked to different forms of epilepsy. Many epilepsy patients with hemizygous NaV1.1 loss of function display ataxia and motor delays and deficiencies (Claes et al., 2001; Fujiwara et al., 2003), which has traditionally been attributed to loss of NaV1.1 function in the brain, namely, the cerebellum (Kalume et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: Cited from published literature (Claes et al., 2001; Fujiwara et al., 2003).

claims.claim: Motor deficits in epilepsy patients have traditionally been attributed to loss of NaV1.1 function in the brain, namely, the cerebellum.
claims.source: Many epilepsy patients with hemizygous NaV1.1 loss of function display ataxia and motor delays and deficiencies (Claes et al., 2001; Fujiwara et al., 2003), which has traditionally been attributed to loss of NaV1.1 function in the brain, namely, the cerebellum (Kalume et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: Cited from published literature (Kalume et al., 2007).

claims.claim: NaV1.1 in proprioceptors is a dominant functional NaV subtype.
claims.source: Collectively, these data suggest that in proprioceptors NaV1.1 is a dominant functional NaV subtype.
claims.evidence: Inferred from serial pharmacological blockade experiments showing NaV1.1 comprises 44.8% of the whole-cell sodium current.

claims.claim: NaV1.1 is required for transmission of receptor potentials generated during sustained muscle stretch.
claims.source: This suggests that while a combination of Piezo2 and other NaV isoforms is sufficient to elicit activity in response to transient stimuli, NaV1.1 is required for transmission of receptor potentials generated during sustained muscle stretch.
claims.evidence: Inferred from ex vivo recordings showing impaired static but not dynamic sensitivity in Scn1a-cKO afferents.

claims.claim: NaV1.1 haploinsufficiency in sensory neurons impairs both proprioceptor function and motor behaviors.
claims.source: Impressively, recordings from afferents of heterozygous conditional knockout animals were similarly impaired, and heterozygous conditional knockout mice also exhibited motor behavioral deficits. Thus, NaV1.1 haploinsufficiency in sensory neurons impairs both proprioceptor function and motor behaviors.
claims.evidence: Supported by ex vivo recordings and behavioral data from Scn1a-Het mice.

claims.claim: Sensory neuron dysfunction contributes to the clinical manifestations of neurological disorders in which NaV1.1 function is compromised.
claims.source: Importantly, human patients harboring NaV1.1 loss-of-function mutations often present with motor delays and ataxia; therefore, our data suggest that sensory neuron dysfunction contributes to the clinical manifestations of neurological disorders in which NaV1.1 function is compromised.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the findings in mouse models and known clinical presentations in human patients.

claims.claim: NaV1.1 is essential for mammalian proprioceptive signaling and behaviors.
claims.source: Collectively, we present the first evidence that NaV1.1 is essential for mammalian proprioceptive signaling and behaviors.
claims.evidence: Conclusion drawn from the combined data of expression analysis, electrophysiology, and behavioral experiments.

claims.claim: Some proprioceptor subtypes rely more heavily on NaV1.6 and NaV1.7 for electrical activity.
claims.source: In line with this, pharmacological inhibition of NaV1.1 is sufficient to significantly attenuate action potential firing in most proprioceptors; yet, it should be noted that 25% of the neurons we recorded fired action potentials that were insensitive to ICA application. This suggests that some proprioceptor subtypes rely more heavily on NaV1.6 and NaV1.7 for electrical activity.
claims.evidence: Inferred from current-clamp experiments showing 25% of proprioceptors were insensitive to ICA.

claims.claim: NaV1.1 has a specific role in proprioceptor responses to static muscle movement.
claims.source: These results, however, should be interpreted with the caveat that in these experiments ICA may also be acting on NaV1.3 channels that are upregulated during DRG neuron culturing (Wangzhou et al., 2020). Nevertheless, at the afferent level Scn1a-cKO and Scn1a-Het animals show clear deficits in static stretch sensitivity, but not dynamic sensitivity, and could even entrain to vibrations as fast as 100 Hz, suggesting a specific role for NaV1.1 in proprioceptors responses to static muscle movement.
claims.evidence: Inferred from ex vivo recordings showing impaired static but not dynamic sensitivity.

claims.claim: The observed motor behavioral deficits in Scn1a-cKO mice are likely due to reduced static sensitivity of proprioceptor afferents.
claims.source: Finally, we found that loss of NaV1.1 in sensory neurons had no effect on proprioceptor development, muscle spindle morphology, or proprioceptive afferent innervation of ChAT+ motor neurons in the spinal cord. Thus, the observed motor behavioral deficits are likely due to reduced static sensitivity of proprioceptor afferents.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the absence of developmental deficits and the presence of functional deficits in static sensitivity.

claims.claim: During dynamic or vibratory stimuli, Piezo2 and likely a combination of other molecular mediators, including NaV1.6 and NaV1.7, are sufficient to elicit normal electrical activity.
claims.source: Our model proposes that NaV1.1 is tasked with maintaining consistent firing in spindle afferents during static muscle stretch for normal motor behaviors, whereby activation of the mechanotransduction channel Piezo2 initiates electrical signaling, which in turn activates a complement of TTX-sensitive NaV channels (Carrasco et al., 2017; Florez-Paz et al., 2016; Woo et al., 2015; Figure 10). During dynamic or vibratory stimuli, Piezo2, and likely a combination of other molecular mediators, including NaV1.6 and NaV1.7, are sufficient to elicit normal electrical activity.
claims.evidence: Proposed model based on experimental findings and cited literature (Carrasco et al., 2017; Florez-Paz et al., 2016; Woo et al., 2015).

claims.claim: During prolonged muscle stretch when Piezo2 channels presumably inactivate, NaV1.1 is required for regular and reliable firing.
claims.source: Conversely, during prolonged muscle stretch when Piezo2 channels presumably inactivate, NaV1.1 is required for regular and reliable firing.
claims.evidence: Proposed model based on experimental findings showing impaired static but not dynamic sensitivity.

claims.claim: Vesicle-released glutamate contributes to mammalian proprioception.
claims.source: While other signaling molecules and channels, such as vesicle-released glutamate (Bewick et al., 2005; Than et al., 2021), and mechanosensitive ASIC channels (Lin et al., 2016) and ENaC channels (Bewick and Banks, 2015), also contribute to mammalian proprioception, our data suggests that NaV1.1 is a critical for muscle spindle afferent mechanotransduction, given the overt behavioral deficits observed in Scn1a-cKO mice.
claims.evidence: Cited from published literature (Bewick et al., 2005; Than et al., 2021).

claims.claim: Mechanosensitive ASIC channels contribute to mammalian proprioception.
claims.source: While other signaling molecules and channels, such as vesicle-released glutamate (Bewick et al., 2005; Than et al., 2021), and mechanosensitive ASIC channels (Lin et al., 2016) and ENaC channels (Bewick and Banks, 2015), also contribute to mammalian proprioception, our data suggests that NaV1.1 is a critical for muscle spindle afferent mechanotransduction, given the overt behavioral deficits observed in Scn1a-cKO mice.
claims.evidence: Cited from published literature (Lin et al., 2016).

claims.claim: ENaC channels contribute to mammalian proprioception.
claims.source: While other signaling molecules and channels, such as vesicle-released glutamate (Bewick et al., 2005; Than et al., 2021), and mechanosensitive ASIC channels (Lin et al., 2016) and ENaC channels (Bewick and Banks, 2015), also contribute to mammalian proprioception, our data suggests that NaV1.1 is a critical for muscle spindle afferent mechanotransduction, given the overt behavioral deficits observed in Scn1a-cKO mice.
claims.evidence: Cited from published literature (Bewick and Banks, 2015).

claims.claim: NaV1.1 is critical for muscle spindle afferent mechanotransduction.
claims.source: While other signaling molecules and channels, such as vesicle-released glutamate (Bewick et al., 2005; Than et al., 2021), and mechanosensitive ASIC channels (Lin et al., 2016) and ENaC channels (Bewick and Banks, 2015), also contribute to mammalian proprioception, our data suggests that NaV1.1 is a critical for muscle spindle afferent mechanotransduction, given the overt behavioral deficits observed in Scn1a-cKO mice.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the overt behavioral deficits observed in Scn1a-cKO mice.

claims.claim: Alterations in Golgi tendon organ function likely contribute to the behavioral deficits observed in Scn1a-cKO mice.
claims.source: Due to the ubiquitous expression of NaV1.1 in all proprioceptors and the importance of Golgi tendon organ (GTO) feedback to motor control, alterations in function in those proprioceptors likely contribute to the behavioral deficits we observed; however, we did not directly measure their function.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the ubiquitous expression of NaV1.1 in proprioceptors and the known importance of GTOs.

claims.claim: ICA 121431 also blocks NaV1.3 channels.
claims.source: It is important to note that ICA 121431 also blocks NaV1.3 channels, which could be upregulated in our cultured DRG neuron preparations (Wangzhou et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: Cited from published literature (Wangzhou et al., 2020).

claims.claim: A small but significant decrease in INa was observed in recordings from large-diameter DRG neurons harvested from Scn1a-cKO mice following ICA application (p=0.0041).
claims.source: Indeed, a small but significant decrease in INa was observed in recordings from large-diameter DRG neurons harvested from PirtCre;Scn1a-floxed mice (Scn1a-cKO), which lack NaV1.1 in all sensory neurons. Thus, inhibition of upregulated NaV1.3 channels could contribute to the effect of on ICA on the proprioceptor INa(Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: Determined by voltage-clamp experiments in Scn1a-cKO neurons shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Deletion of NaV1.1 in small- and medium-diameter DRG neurons using a peripherin-Cre driver did not produce visible motor deficits.
claims.source: Deletion of NaV1.1 in small- and medium-diameter DRG neurons using a peripherin-Cre driver did not produce visible motor deficits (Osteen et al., 2016), indicating that sensory neuron populations in those categories are not involved.
claims.evidence: Cited from published literature (Osteen et al., 2016).

claims.claim: Baseline mechanical thresholds were unchanged following intraplantar injection of a selective NaV1.1 inhibitor.
claims.source: Notably, baseline mechanical thresholds were unchanged following intraplantar injection of a selective NaV1.1 inhibitor (Salvatierra et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: Cited from published literature (Salvatierra et al., 2018).

claims.claim: Functional NaV1.1 protein may only be upregulated in tactile sensory neurons during pathological states.
claims.source: This suggests that while NaV1.1 mRNA is expressed in most tactile sensory neurons, functional protein may only be upregulated in these populations during pathological states.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation that NaV1.1 inhibition does not affect baseline mechanical thresholds.

claims.claim: Loss of less than a quarter of the proprioceptor INa is sufficient to impair proprioceptor responsiveness to muscle stretch.
claims.source: At the afferent level, heterozygous and homozygous loss of NaV1.1 produced similar deficits in static firing, suggesting that loss of less than a quarter of the proprioceptor INa is sufficient to impair proprioceptor responsiveness to muscle stretch.
claims.evidence: Inferred from ex vivo recordings showing similar deficits in Scn1a-Het and Scn1a-cKO afferents.

claims.claim: Loss of presynaptic NaV1.7 channels in the spinal cord reduced glutamate release from nociceptive afferents onto dorsal horn neurons.
claims.source: For example, loss of presynaptic NaV1.7 channels in the spinal cord reduced glutamate release from nociceptive afferents onto dorsal horn neurons (MacDonald et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: Cited from published literature (MacDonald et al., 2021).

claims.claim: Some of the clinical manifestations associated with epilepsy may manifest in part as a result of unreliable coding by peripheral proprioceptors.
claims.source: Notably, Scn1a is a super culprit gene with over 1000 associated disease-causing mutations, most of which are linked to different forms of epilepsy. Many epilepsy patients with hemizygous NaV1.1 loss of function display ataxia and motor delays and deficiencies (Claes et al., 2001; Fujiwara et al., 2003), which has traditionally been attributed to loss of NaV1.1 function in the brain, namely, the cerebellum (Kalume et al., 2007). Our findings suggest that some of the clinical manifestations associated with epilepsy are not solely due to NaV1.1 loss of function in the brain, but also may manifest in part as a result of unreliable coding by peripheral proprioceptors.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the findings in mouse models showing proprioceptor dysfunction and motor deficits.

claims.claim: There are anywhere from 5 to 8 different proprioceptor molecular subclasses.
claims.source: There are anywhere from 5 to 8 different proprioceptor molecular subclasses (Oliver et al., 2021; Wu et al., 2021), however, and it is possible that these distinct classes rely on different combinations of these channels for function.
claims.evidence: Cited from published literature (Oliver et al., 2021; Wu et al., 2021).

claims.claim: Distinct proprioceptor subclasses may rely on different combinations of NaV channels for function.
claims.source: There are anywhere from 5 to 8 different proprioceptor molecular subclasses (Oliver et al., 2021; Wu et al., 2021), however, and it is possible that these distinct classes rely on different combinations of these channels for function.
claims.evidence: Speculated based on the existence of multiple proprioceptor subclasses and observed variability in NaV expression.

claims.claim: NaV1.1 may be localized to muscle spindle afferent endings where it helps amplify receptor current.
claims.source: NaV1.1 has been localized to muscle spindle afferent endings and has been hypothesized to help amplify receptor current (Carrasco et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: Cited from published literature (Carrasco et al., 2017).

claims.claim: Amplification of the receptor potential by NaV1.1 is necessary to maintain firing during held stretch.
claims.source: Our results support a model whereby current from Piezo2 and potentially other mechanically sensitive ion channels at the start of stretch produces a sufficient receptor potential to generate firing at the heminode, but that amplification of the receptor potential by NaV1.1 is necessary to maintain firing during held stretch.
claims.evidence: Proposed model based on experimental findings showing impaired static sensitivity in Scn1a-cKO afferents.

claims.claim: Glutamate may play a more general role in maintaining excitability in proprioceptor afferents.
claims.source: A similar deficit in static but not dynamic sensitivity was seen following loss of synaptic-like vesicle released glutamate from afferent endings (Than et al., 2021); however, in those afferents, firing only occurred at the beginning of stretch and patchy firing was never observed. This may indicate that glutamate plays a more general role maintaining excitability, whereas NaV1.1 is required for reliable action potential generation at heminodes during static stimuli.
claims.evidence: Inferred from comparison with published findings (Than et al., 2021) and current results.

claims.claim: NaV1.1 is required for reliable action potential generation at heminodes during static stimuli.
claims.source: This may indicate that glutamate plays a more general role maintaining excitability, whereas NaV1.1 is required for reliable action potential generation at heminodes during static stimuli.
claims.evidence: Inferred from experimental findings showing impaired static sensitivity in Scn1a-cKO afferents.

claims.claim: NaV1.1 expressed along the axon could be essential for sustained static firing.
claims.source: Alternatively, or in addition, NaV1.1 expressed along the axon could be essential for sustained static firing.
claims.evidence: Speculated as an alternative mechanism for NaV1.1's role in static firing.

claims.claim: The lack of an effect on dynamic sensitivity could suggest the upregulation of other NaV subtypes or other molecules as a compensatory mechanism to counteract the loss of NaV1.1.
claims.source: The lack of an effect on dynamic sensitivity could suggest the upregulation of other NaV subtypes or other molecules as a compensatory mechanism to counteract the loss of NaV1.1.

claims.claim: Loss of proprioceptor activity does not generally reduce proprioceptive input into the spinal cord.
claims.source: Additionally, we did not observe a general decrease in α-motor neuron innervation, which is consistent with the findings of Mendelsohn et al., 2015, who reported loss of proprioceptor activity does not generally reduce proprioceptive input into the spinal cord.
claims.evidence: Cited from published literature (Mendelsohn et al., 2015).

claims.claim: Loss of proprioceptor transmission causes changes in heteronymous sensory-motor connectivity, whereby proprioceptor innervation of motor neurons that project to antagonistic muscles is increased.
claims.source: Interestingly, however, the authors did observe changes in heteronymous sensory-motor connectivity when proprioceptor transmission was blocked, whereby proprioceptor innervation of motor neurons that project to antagonistic muscles was increased.
claims.evidence: Cited from published literature (Mendelsohn et al., 2015).

claims.claim: Loss of NaV1.1 in proprioceptive afferents may cause them to 'mis-wire' and make connections with inappropriate motor neuron pools.
claims.source: Whether loss of NaV1.1 in proprioceptive afferents causes them to 'mis-wire' in our model to make connections with inappropriate motor neuron pools is unclear.
claims.evidence: Speculated as a possible mechanism contributing to behavioral deficits.

results.result: NaV1.1 (Scn1a) is ubiquitously expressed in proprioceptors and myelinated neurons, but shows low expression in nociceptors. RNAscope analysis revealed that 93% of myelinated neurons and 100% of genetically identified proprioceptors express Scn1a mRNA, while only 24% of CGRP+ peptidergic nociceptors and 3% of Mrgprd+ non-peptidergic nociceptors express this channel.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C4 are well-supported by RNAscope data with clear quantification shown in Figures 1A-D. The methodology using genetic reporters (PvalbAi14) and specific markers (NFH, CGRP, Mrgprd) provides robust cell-type identification. Sample sizes appear adequate (n=153-877 cells), and the pie chart quantifications clearly show the percentage of positive cells in each population.

results.result: NaV1.1, NaV1.6, and NaV1.7 are all ubiquitously expressed in proprioceptors, but NaV1.1 shows the most consistent and highest expression levels. All three channels are present in 100% of proprioceptors, but NaV1.1 has the lowest coefficient of variation (75.6 vs 97.3 for NaV1.6 and 88.1 for NaV1.7) and significantly higher average integrated density (p<0.0001).
results.evaluation: Claims C5-C11 are supported by comprehensive RNAscope analysis shown in Figures 1-2. The use of coefficient of variation to assess expression consistency is appropriate, and the statistical comparison of integrated densities (Kruskal-Wallis with Dunn's post-hoc) is properly conducted. The data converge to show NaV1.1 as the dominant and most consistently expressed isoform in proprioceptors.

results.result: Serial pharmacological blockade reveals that NaV1.1 is the dominant functional sodium channel subtype in proprioceptors, comprising 44.8% of the whole-cell sodium current. NaV1.6 and NaV1.7 contribute 14.5% and 32.9% respectively, with 7.8% remaining unblocked due to incomplete drug efficacy.
results.evaluation: Claims C12-C15 are supported by well-designed serial pharmacological experiments (Figure 2F-G) using selective antagonists. The experimental logic is sound: blocking NaV1.1 first, then NaV1.6 (accounting for partial NaV1.1 block by AH-TTX), then NaV1.7, and finally TTX. However, a caveat exists: ICA 121431 may also block NaV1.3, which could be upregulated in culture (acknowledged by authors in C104-C105). This doesn't invalidate the result but introduces uncertainty about the precise contribution.

results.result: Proprioceptor sodium currents exhibit characteristic biophysical properties including voltage-dependent activation (V50 = -38.7 mV), inactivation (midpoint = -64.5 mV), rapid recovery from fast inactivation (τ = 0.54 ms with >50% recovery at 0.5 ms), and slow entry into slow inactivation (τ = 928.6 ms with >50% channels available after 2000 ms).
results.evaluation: Claims C17-C24 are supported by standard voltage-clamp protocols shown in Figure 3. The biophysical characterization is comprehensive and uses appropriate methods (Boltzmann fitting, exponential curve fitting). Sample sizes appear adequate (n=6-12 cells for different protocols). These represent the first reported biophysical properties of proprioceptor sodium currents, as stated by the authors.

results.result: Pharmacological blockade of NaV1.1 with ICA 121431 significantly reduces proprioceptor sodium current density from ~-140 to ~-75 pA/pF (p=0.0003) and slows current decay kinetics from 0.6 to 1.0 ms (p=0.0007), without affecting rise time. The ICA-sensitive component has an average tau of 0.4 ms and current density of -96 pA/pF, with substantial variability across cells (-28 to -263 pA/pF).
results.evaluation: Claims C25-C30 are supported by voltage-clamp data in Figure 4A-E with appropriate statistical tests (Wilcoxon matched-pairs). The wide distribution of ICA-sensitive current densities (C30) is an important observation suggesting proprioceptor subtype heterogeneity. However, the caveat about potential NaV1.3 blockade (C104-C105) applies here as well, though the authors address this with experiments in Scn1a-cKO neurons showing only a small residual ICA effect.

results.result: Pharmacological inhibition of NaV1.1 significantly impairs proprioceptor intrinsic excitability, reducing the number of evoked action potentials in most cells, decreasing action potential amplitude (p=0.0420) and threshold (p=0.0186), and increasing action potential width (p=0.0068). However, 25% of proprioceptors (5 cells) with low firing rates were insensitive to ICA.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C35 are supported by current-clamp experiments in Figure 4F-K with appropriate paired statistical tests. The observation that 25% of cells are ICA-insensitive (C32) is important and suggests proprioceptor subtype heterogeneity. The changes in action potential properties are consistent with loss of a fast-gating sodium channel. Sample size (n=20 cells) is adequate for these experiments.

results.result: Scn1a-cKO mice display profound motor abnormalities including ataxic-like tremors, abnormal limb positioning, and paw clasping, which are absent in Scn1a-floxed controls and Scn1a-Het mice. These phenotypes are visible and documented in videos and images.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C40 are supported by behavioral observations documented in Videos 1-3 and Figure 5A. The phenotypes are clearly visible and distinct from controls. The observation that heterozygous animals do not show these overt motor abnormalities (C40) is important for distinguishing severity of phenotypes. The use of both sexes strengthens the findings.

results.result: In the open-field test, both Scn1a-cKO and Scn1a-Het mice show significant motor deficits compared to controls, traveling less distance and moving slower (p<0.01 for both genotypes). However, time spent moving and time in center are unchanged, suggesting gross motor function and anxiety-like behavior are intact.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C46 are supported by open-field behavioral data in Figure 5B-F with appropriate statistical tests (one-way ANOVA with Dunnett's post-hoc). The finding that heterozygous animals show deficits in this assay (C43-C44) is particularly important, demonstrating haploinsufficiency. Sample sizes are adequate (N=6-15 animals). The lack of effect on time moving (C45) and center time (C46) helps rule out confounding factors.

results.result: On the rotarod test, Scn1a-cKO mice perform significantly worse than Scn1a-floxed and Scn1a-Het mice, maintaining position for only 41 seconds on average by day 3. In contrast, Scn1a-Het mice perform similarly to controls, indicating no haploinsufficiency in this assay.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C49 are supported by rotarod data in Figure 5G-H with appropriate statistical tests (two-way mixed-design ANOVA with Dunnett's post-hoc). The differential effect between open-field and rotarod for heterozygous animals is intriguing and suggests these assays measure different aspects of motor function. Sample sizes are adequate (N=11-20 animals). The lack of haploinsufficiency in rotarod contrasts with open-field results.

results.result: No sex-dependent differences were observed in either open-field or rotarod behavioral tests, indicating that motor deficits in Scn1a-cKO and Scn1a-Het mice are consistent across sexes.
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C51 are supported by sex-stratified analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1. The inclusion of both sexes and explicit testing for sex differences strengthens the study. Sample sizes appear adequate (males n=10-18, females n=17-24 depending on test).

results.result: The PirtCre driver selectively targets sensory neurons, with little-to-no neuronal TdTomato expression in spinal cord but strong labeling in DRG somata and axons, confirming the specificity of the genetic model.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C53 are supported by immunohistochemistry data in Figure 5—figure supplement 2. This is an important control demonstrating that the behavioral phenotypes are due to sensory neuron-specific deletion rather than CNS effects. The imaging is clear and convincing, though quantification would strengthen the claim. Sample size (N=3 mice, n=30 sections) is adequate for this qualitative assessment.

results.result: Loss of NaV1.1 does not affect proprioceptor development, as the number of Pvalb+/Runx3+ proprioceptors per DRG section is unchanged between Scn1a-floxed, Scn1a-Het, and Scn1a-cKO mice (p=0.3824 and p=0.1665 respectively).
results.evaluation: Claim C54 is supported by RNAscope quantification in Figure 6 using appropriate markers (Pvalb and Runx3) for mature proprioceptors. Statistical analysis (Kruskal-Wallis with Dunn's post-hoc) is appropriate. Sample sizes are adequate (n=17-18 sections). This is an important control ruling out developmental defects as the cause of behavioral phenotypes.

results.result: Muscle spindle morphology is normal in Scn1a-cKO mice, with no qualitative differences observed between genotypes, similar to findings in conditional Piezo2-knockout animals.
results.evaluation: Claim C55 is supported by muscle spindle whole mount analysis in Figure 6—figure supplement 1. The comparison to Piezo2-knockout animals (Woo et al., 2015) provides useful context. However, the analysis is qualitative rather than quantitative, which limits the strength of the conclusion. Sample sizes are adequate (n=7-9 spindles). Quantitative morphometric analysis would strengthen this result.

results.result: Proprioceptive innervation of spinal motor neurons is intact in Scn1a-cKO mice, with no significant decrease in VGLUT1 puncta density on ChAT+ neurons compared to controls (p>0.9999 for Het, p=0.4573 for cKO).
results.evaluation: Claim C56 is supported by quantitative immunohistochemistry in Figure 7 with appropriate statistical analysis (Kruskal-Wallis with Dunn's post-hoc). The methodology of analyzing large ChAT+ neurons (>400 μm²) to bias toward α-motor neurons is reasonable. Sample sizes are excellent (n=92-102 neurons). This is an important control ruling out gross connectivity defects.

results.result: Ex vivo muscle afferent recordings reveal that loss of NaV1.1 severely impairs static stretch sensitivity in proprioceptors. Afferents from Scn1a-Het and Scn1a-cKO mice show inconsistent firing during the 4-second hold phase of stretch, with significantly increased coefficient of variation of interspike intervals (p=0.015). Almost all control afferents fire consistently throughout stretch, while knockout afferents show action potential failures.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C61 are strongly supported by ex vivo recordings in Figure 8A-D with appropriate statistical analysis (two-way ANOVA). The use of coefficient of variation to quantify firing inconsistency is appropriate. Sample sizes are adequate (n=10-12 afferents per genotype). The finding that both heterozygous and homozygous knockouts show similar deficits is important for demonstrating haploinsufficiency at the cellular level. The pie charts clearly show the proportion of afferents with consistent vs. inconsistent firing.

results.result: Dynamic sensitivity of proprioceptor afferents is preserved in Scn1a-cKO mice, with maximum firing frequency during the rampup phase (Dynamic Peak) being independent of genotype (p=0.0633) and even trending slightly higher in knockout afferents.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C63 are supported by ex vivo recordings in Figure 8E with appropriate statistical analysis (two-way ANOVA). The preservation of dynamic sensitivity while static sensitivity is impaired is a key finding that suggests NaV1.1 has a specific role in sustained firing rather than transient responses. The p-value of 0.0633 is close to significance, and the trend toward higher dynamic peak in knockouts is interesting but requires cautious interpretation.

results.result: Proprioceptor afferents lacking NaV1.1 can entrain to sinusoidal vibration as effectively as control afferents, maintaining firing throughout 9-second vibrations at frequencies up to 100 Hz. Firing rates during vibration are not significantly different between genotypes.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C66 are supported by ex vivo recordings during sinusoidal vibration in Figure 9 and Tables 1-3. Statistical analysis is appropriate (one-way ANOVA and Kruskal-Wallis). Sample sizes are adequate (n=9-11 afferents). The contrast between impaired static firing and preserved dynamic/vibratory responses is striking and supports the authors' model that NaV1.1 is specifically required for sustained firing during static stretch.

results.result: NaV1.1 is a dominant functional sodium channel subtype in proprioceptors, as inferred from its contribution of 44.8% to the whole-cell sodium current.
results.evaluation: Claim C88 is a reasonable inference from the pharmacological data (C12), though the term 'dominant' could be debated since NaV1.1 comprises less than half of the total current. However, it is the single largest contributor among the three isoforms examined. The caveat about potential NaV1.3 blockade should be considered.

results.result: NaV1.1 is specifically required for transmission of receptor potentials generated during sustained muscle stretch, while other NaV isoforms and Piezo2 are sufficient for responses to transient stimuli.
results.evaluation: Claim C89 is a well-supported inference from the ex vivo recordings showing impaired static but preserved dynamic sensitivity (C57-C66). The model is consistent with all the electrophysiological data. However, this is an interpretive claim rather than directly demonstrated, as the authors did not directly measure receptor potentials or manipulate Piezo2.

results.result: NaV1.1 shows haploinsufficiency in sensory neurons for both proprioceptor function and motor behaviors, as demonstrated by similar impairments in Scn1a-Het and Scn1a-cKO mice in ex vivo recordings and open-field tests.
results.evaluation: Claim C90 is strongly supported by convergent evidence from ex vivo recordings (C57-C61) and open-field behavior (C43-C44). The haploinsufficiency is clearly demonstrated at both cellular and behavioral levels. However, it's important to note that haploinsufficiency was not observed in the rotarod test (C47), suggesting task-dependent effects.

results.result: Sensory neuron dysfunction contributes to the clinical manifestations of neurological disorders in which NaV1.1 function is compromised, as suggested by the motor deficits observed in mouse models and the known presentation of motor delays and ataxia in human patients with NaV1.1 mutations.
results.evaluation: Claim C91 is a reasonable inference connecting the mouse data to human disease, but it remains speculative. The authors provide evidence that sensory neuron-specific loss of NaV1.1 causes motor deficits in mice, and cite literature showing human patients with NaV1.1 mutations have motor problems (C86). However, direct evidence that sensory neuron dysfunction contributes to human disease phenotypes is lacking. This is an important hypothesis-generating result that requires future validation in human studies.

results.result: NaV1.1 is essential for mammalian proprioceptive signaling and behaviors, representing the first evidence for this role of the channel.
results.evaluation: Claim C92 is supported by the comprehensive set of data including expression analysis (C1-C11), electrophysiology (C12-C35, C57-C66), and behavior (C36-C49). The convergent evidence from multiple experimental approaches strongly supports this conclusion. The claim of being 'first evidence' appears accurate based on the literature review provided.

results.result: Some proprioceptor subtypes rely more heavily on NaV1.6 and NaV1.7 for electrical activity, as inferred from the observation that 25% of recorded proprioceptors were insensitive to ICA 121431 and had lower intrinsic excitability.
results.evaluation: Claim C94 is a reasonable inference from the observation that 25% of proprioceptors were ICA-insensitive (C32). The correlation with lower firing rates supports the interpretation. However, this is based on a small number of cells (5 out of 20) and could benefit from additional characterization of these ICA-insensitive cells.

results.result: NaV1.1 has a specific role in proprioceptor responses to static muscle movement, as evidenced by clear deficits in static stretch sensitivity but preserved dynamic sensitivity and ability to entrain to vibrations up to 100 Hz.
results.evaluation: Claim C95 is strongly supported by the ex vivo recording data (C57-C66). The dissociation between static and dynamic responses is clear and reproducible. The authors appropriately acknowledge the caveat about potential NaV1.3 involvement in cultured neurons, but the in vivo recordings from Scn1a-cKO afferents confirm the specificity.

results.result: The motor behavioral deficits in Scn1a-cKO mice are likely due to reduced static sensitivity of proprioceptor afferents rather than developmental abnormalities, as proprioceptor number, muscle spindle morphology, and spinal connectivity are all normal.
results.evaluation: Claim C96 is well-supported by the combination of normal developmental markers (C54-C56) and clear functional deficits (C57-C66). The logic is sound: since development is normal but function is impaired, the behavioral deficits likely result from functional impairment. However, this remains an inference, and other functional deficits not examined (e.g., in Golgi tendon organs, acknowledged in C103) could also contribute.

results.result: The authors propose a model where Piezo2 and other NaV isoforms (NaV1.6, NaV1.7) are sufficient for dynamic/vibratory responses, while NaV1.1 is specifically required for maintaining firing during prolonged static stretch when Piezo2 presumably inactivates.
results.evaluation: Claims C97-C98 represent a mechanistic model that is well-supported by the data, though it includes speculative elements (e.g., the timing of Piezo2 inactivation). The model is consistent with all experimental observations and provides a coherent framework for understanding NaV1.1's role. However, direct testing of Piezo2 inactivation kinetics during stretch would strengthen the model. The model is appropriately presented as a proposal rather than proven fact.

results.result: NaV1.1 is critical for muscle spindle afferent mechanotransduction, as evidenced by the overt behavioral deficits in Scn1a-cKO mice despite normal development and connectivity.
results.evaluation: Claim C102 is supported by the convergent evidence from behavior, electrophysiology, and developmental analyses. The term 'critical' is justified by the severity of the phenotype. However, the authors acknowledge that other channels (glutamate receptors, ASIC, ENaC) also contribute to proprioception (C99-C101), so NaV1.1 is critical but not the only important component.

results.result: Alterations in Golgi tendon organ (GTO) function likely contribute to the behavioral deficits in Scn1a-cKO mice, given the ubiquitous expression of NaV1.1 in all proprioceptors and the importance of GTO feedback to motor control, though this was not directly measured.
results.evaluation: Claim C103 is speculative and acknowledged as such by the authors. While the reasoning is sound (NaV1.1 is expressed in all proprioceptors including GTOs, and GTOs are important for motor control), the lack of direct functional measurements of GTOs makes this uncertain. This represents an important limitation and direction for future work.

results.result: Loss of less than a quarter of the proprioceptor sodium current is sufficient to impair proprioceptor responsiveness to muscle stretch, as inferred from the similar deficits in heterozygous and homozygous knockouts despite heterozygotes presumably having ~50% NaV1.1 expression.
results.evaluation: Claim C109 is a reasonable inference from the haploinsufficiency data (C57-C61, C90). The logic is that if heterozygotes have ~50% NaV1.1 expression and NaV1.1 comprises ~45% of total sodium current, then heterozygotes lose ~22.5% of total current. The similar functional deficits in Het and cKO suggest this level of loss is sufficient to impair function. However, this assumes linear relationships between gene dosage, protein expression, and current, which may not hold.

results.result: Some clinical manifestations of epilepsy associated with NaV1.1 mutations may result from unreliable coding by peripheral proprioceptors rather than solely from CNS dysfunction, as suggested by the motor deficits in sensory neuron-specific knockout mice.
results.evaluation: Claim C111 is a speculative but well-reasoned inference. The authors show that sensory neuron-specific loss of NaV1.1 causes motor deficits in mice, and cite literature showing epilepsy patients with NaV1.1 mutations have motor problems traditionally attributed to cerebellar dysfunction (C86-C87). This suggests peripheral contributions may be underappreciated. However, this remains a hypothesis requiring validation in human studies or models that can dissect peripheral vs. central contributions.

results.result: ICA 121431 also blocks NaV1.3 channels, which may be upregulated in cultured DRG neurons. A small but significant ICA-sensitive current (p=0.0041) was observed in Scn1a-cKO neurons, suggesting some contribution of NaV1.3 to the ICA effect in culture.
results.evaluation: Claims C104-C105 represent an important caveat acknowledged by the authors. The data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 show a small residual ICA effect in Scn1a-cKO neurons, supporting the possibility of NaV1.3 involvement. This is appropriately disclosed and doesn't invalidate the main findings, as the ex vivo recordings from Scn1a-cKO afferents (which don't involve culture) confirm the role of NaV1.1. The authors could have strengthened this by testing NaV1.3 expression in cultured vs. fresh neurons.

results.result: The authors propose that amplification of the receptor potential by NaV1.1 is necessary to maintain firing during held stretch, with Piezo2 and other mechanosensitive channels providing sufficient initial depolarization to trigger firing at the heminode.
results.evaluation: Claim C115 is a mechanistic model supported by the data, particularly the dissociation between preserved dynamic and impaired static responses. The model is consistent with prior work showing NaV1.1 localization to muscle spindle endings (C114). However, this is an interpretive framework rather than directly demonstrated mechanism. Direct measurements of receptor potentials and NaV1.1 localization in the specific experimental animals would strengthen this model.

results.result: The authors propose that glutamate plays a general role in maintaining excitability in proprioceptor afferents, while NaV1.1 is specifically required for reliable action potential generation at heminodes during static stimuli, based on comparison with published glutamate knockout data.
results.evaluation: Claims C116-C117 are speculative comparisons with published work (Than et al., 2021). While the comparison is interesting and the reasoning is plausible, the differences in phenotypes (patchy firing in NaV1.1 knockouts vs. firing only at stretch onset in glutamate knockouts) could have multiple explanations. Direct experimental comparison or combined manipulations would be needed to test this model.

results.result: The authors provide extensive literature context establishing prior knowledge about NaV1.1 in brain disease, peripheral sensory neurons, pain signaling, and other cell types, as well as the roles of other channels in proprioception.
results.evaluation: These claims (C67-C87, C99-C101, C106-C107, C110, C112, C114, C120-C121) are citations of published literature and established knowledge. They are appropriately referenced and provide important context for the study. The accuracy of these citations would need to be verified against the original sources, but they appear to be standard and well-accepted findings in the field.

results.result: The authors propose several speculative mechanisms and hypotheses including: functional NaV1.1 protein may only be upregulated in tactile neurons during pathological states; distinct proprioceptor subclasses may rely on different NaV channel combinations; NaV1.1 along the axon could be essential for sustained firing; upregulation of other channels may compensate for NaV1.1 loss in dynamic responses; and loss of NaV1.1 may cause proprioceptive afferents to 'mis-wire' to inappropriate motor neuron pools.
results.evaluation: Claims C108, C113, C118, C119, and C122 are explicitly speculative hypotheses proposed by the authors. They are reasonable interpretations of the data and represent important directions for future research, but they lack direct experimental support in the current study. The authors appropriately present these as possibilities rather than conclusions.
